transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, honestly, I'm only here because of my work physical. You see, I'm a mechanic down at the dealership, and they make us do these routine physicals every year to make sure we're fit for the job, lifting heavy parts, being on our feet all day, that sort of thing. I went in last week, feeling totally fine, you know, actually feeling pretty good, but the doctor there made this huge deal out of my weight. He kept saying it's way too low, looking at his charts and shaking his head. He practically demanded I come see someone about it, which I think is a bit of an overreaction, to be perfectly honest with you. 

I mean, from my perspective, I feel great. I play in this Wednesday night basketball league with some of the guys from the shop and a few buddies from high school, and since I've dropped a few pounds, I feel so much lighter on my feet. I can cut faster, I don't get winded as quickly, and my knees don't ache the next day like they used to. And even at work, in the garage, I don't feel so weighed down when I'm bending over the engine bays or rolling under the cars on the creeper. It's hot in there, especially in the summer, and carrying extra weight just makes it miserable. So, I don't really see the problem, but here I am, just trying to get the paperwork sorted so they'll get off my back about it.
Do you think your weight is currently too low?

Well, no, I don't. I really don't. I mean... I know people are worried, sure. The doc at the clinic made that pretty clear, and you know, people just notice when you drop a few belt sizes, right? But honestly, I figure they’re all just making way, way too much of it. 

I mean, if you just think about it logically for a second. If my weight was actually a problem, like a real medical issue, would I still be doing everything I do? I'm at the shop five, sometimes six days a week, doing real heavy manual labor. Pulling tires, hoisting engines, working the breaker bar... you name it. I haven't missed a single shift. I still show up for work every morning, punch the clock, and get the job done just as good, if not better, than the younger guys. 

And it's not like I just crash when I clock out, either. I go home, and I'm not just sitting around on the couch—I take care of what needs doing around the house. Just last weekend I was up on the ladder cleaning out the gutters, mowing the lawn, fixing the latch on the garage door... stuff that takes real energy. And, like I mentioned before, I’m still out there playing ball on weekends and Wednesday nights. Running up and down a full court for an hour straight! You just can't do that if your body is too weak or your weight is dangerously low or whatever it is they think is happening to me. 

So yeah, they can look at their little BMI charts and shake their heads all they want, but as long as I'm working hard, taking care of my house, and playing hard on the court, I just don't see how my weight could possibly be too low. It just doesn't make any sense to me.
Are you afraid of gaining weight?

Well, I mean... afraid is a strong word, you know? It's not like I'm waking up in a cold sweat or anything like that. But, yeah, I guess you could say I really, really don't want to put the weight back on. I mean, why would I? Like I said, I feel so much better now. But it's more than just feeling better, it's... it's this constant thing in the back of my mind. 

I've got this routine, right? I weigh myself every morning, right after I get out of the shower, before I even put my work boots on or have a cup of black coffee. And if I see that number on the scale bump up, even just a single pound, or if I put on my work jeans—the Levi's I've worn for years—and they feel even a tiny bit tighter around the waist, it just messes with my head for the whole rest of the day. 

I start thinking, you know, that I'm getting soft. That I'm losing my edge. I picture myself back under the hood of a Chevy Silverado, trying to contort myself to reach a spark plug in the back of the engine block, and I start worrying that I'm going to be too bulky to fit my arm in there, or that I'll be slower rolling around on the creeper. Or I think about Wednesday nights, and I worry that if I put on weight, I won't be able to keep up with the younger guys on a fast break, that I'll be huffing and puffing by the second quarter like I used to. 

It's just... I've worked hard to get to this point where I'm moving good, where my joints don't hurt as much, and the idea of going backward, of getting heavy and slow again, it just... it really bothers me. So, yeah, I watch it close. I have to. Because in my line of work, and the way I like to play ball, getting soft just isn't an option. You gotta stay lean to stay quick, you know what I mean?
Do you ever restrict what you eat or how much you eat because you're worried about gaining weight?

Well, I mean, "restrict" is kind of a clinical way to put it, I guess. I just... I have my routine, you know? Like I said, I like to stay lean, keep my edge. So, most days, I just don't really eat much. I mean, I get up early, like 5:30, and the first thing I do is put on a pot of coffee. Black, obviously. No sugar, no cream, none of that extra stuff. And honestly, that gets me through the whole morning. I'll take a big thermos of it with me to the dealership, and I'll just sip on that while I'm doing the morning diagnostics, pulling cars into the bays, talking to the service advisors... it keeps me going, keeps me sharp. 

And then, you know, lunchtime rolls around, and the other guys in the shop, they're always ordering out. Pizzas, giant subs, burgers and fries from the place across the street. And they'll ask if I want in, and I just tell them no, I'm good. Because if I eat a big heavy meal like that in the middle of the day, I just know I'm going to feel sluggish all afternoon. I'll be under a car, trying to torque a bolt, and I'll just feel... weighed down, you know? So I usually just bring something small from home. Maybe a small sandwich, like just a thin slice of turkey on wheat, or honestly, half the time I don't even finish it. I'll just eat half of whatever I brought, or half an apple, just enough to stop my stomach from growling so loud the customer can hear it in the waiting room. 

And then by the time I get home, it's usually pretty late. The shop has been crazy busy lately, they're always asking us to stay over and finish up a job so the customer can have their car back the next morning. So I get home, and I'm tired, and I've still got stuff to do around the house, like I was telling you before. Fixing things, yard work, whatever. So I don't really want to sit down and have this huge, elaborate dinner. I just feel better sticking to my own simple rules, you know? Keeping it light. It just makes my life easier, and it keeps me feeling the way I want to feel. I don't really see it as restricting, it's just... it's just how I operate now. It's what works for me.
How much weight have you lost since you started feeling like you needed to be lighter?

Well, as for the exact number, I mean... I wasn't exactly keeping a running tally on a calendar or anything when this all started. It was more of a gradual thing, just trying to get that edge back, like I was telling you. But, well, I guess I know the number now because of my work physical. Actually, that work physical is exactly what got me here talking to you in the first place. 

See, the dealership I work for, they got bought out by this larger corporate auto group a couple of years back, and now they have this strict policy where all the service techs have to go to this specific occupational health clinic over on Route 9 for an annual workup. I guess it's a liability thing for their insurance, making sure we can still lift the tires and operate the heavy machinery, all that stuff. So I go in a few weeks ago, and I do the whole routine—the hearing test, the vision test, the mobility stuff—and then they have me step on the scale. And the doctor there, he looks at my file from last year, looks at the scale, and makes this absolutely huge deal out of it. He said I dropped something like 35 or 40 pounds since my last checkup. 

And he gets this real serious look on his face and tells me that my weight is too low. He actually used those exact words, that it was "too low" and a safety concern, and said I needed to get evaluated, which is, you know, why they made me come see you. But I just sat there looking at him, thinking... how can it possibly be too low? To me, I just feel lighter on my feet! When I'm out there playing basketball, I can actually cut and pivot without my knees screaming, and I don't get winded on a fast break anymore. And at the garage, I don't feel all weighed down and sluggish when I'm reaching over a fender or sliding under a truck on the creeper. I'm moving better than I have in ten years. So he can say it's too low all he wants, and make me jump through these hoops, but honestly, I just feel like I finally dropped the dead weight so I can actually do my job.
Has your concern about gaining weight ever caused problems in your relationships with friends or family?

Well, I mean... it depends on who you ask, I guess. As far as the guys go, like the guys at the shop or the guys I play ball with? No, no problems there. Like I said, I’m still keeping up with the garage just fine, pulling my weight, and I'm still running the floor in my basketball league. Better than I used to, honestly. So they don't care. 

But... well, at home, it's a different story. It’s definitely caused some tension at home. My wife, my family... they just don't really get it. They have this whole routine where they want everyone sitting down at the dining room table for these big, regular family meals. You know the kind of stuff—meatloaf, mashed potatoes, huge plates of baked ziti on a Sunday. And I just... I avoid it. I really do. I'll stay out in the driveway tinkering with the truck, or I'll just tell them I had a late lunch at the dealership, or I'll just grab a piece of plain sliced turkey and eat it standing up at the kitchen counter while they're all sitting down. 

And man, they just make such a huge deal out of it. It’s like they can't just let me be. Every time there's a dinner or a family thing, my wife or my sister, they're always pulling me aside, giving me this worried look, asking if I’m okay. "Are you feeling alright? You look so different, are you sick?" It drives me absolutely up the wall. I mean, I tell them, "I just worked a ten-hour shift on my feet and played three games of full-court pickup, do I look sick to you?" But they just keep harping on it, constantly asking if I'm okay just because I don't want to sit down and stuff my face with a heavy casserole. So, yeah, it causes some arguments, definitely. I just wish they'd back off and see that I'm actually doing what I need to do to stay on top of my game.
Do you ever think about how your body looks when you're deciding what to eat?

Well, looks... I mean, I’m not standing in front of the mirror posing like a bodybuilder or anything, if that’s what you mean. I'm a mechanic, I'm not trying to be on a magazine cover. But, yeah, I do pay attention to it, absolutely. Especially when it comes to my clothes and how I'm carrying myself. 

Like, I have my routine in the morning, right? I get up, I shower, I weigh myself, I put on my jeans or my work pants. And man, if I see the scale bump up even a single pound, or if I put those jeans on and they feel even just a little bit tighter around the waist than they did the day before... it just immediately gets in my head. I start thinking I’m getting soft. And for me, getting soft means losing my edge. I start thinking that if I put that weight back on, I’ll be slower moving around the cars in the bays, or I'll be slower running up and down the court during my basketball games. 

And I just can't have that. I've seen too many guys my age at the dealership just completely let themselves go. You hit your forties and guys just stop caring. They get these big beer guts, and then they're leaning over a customer's car to reach an alternator, scratching the paint with their belt buckle because they can't physically reach over their own stomach anymore. I absolutely refuse to be that guy. 

So, yeah, when I'm looking at what to eat for the day, or if the guys are passing around a menu for lunch, that tight feeling in my jeans or that number on the scale is exactly what I'm thinking about. If I feel like I'm getting even a little bit soft, I just... I skip the meal, or I just stick to my black coffee. I'll just tell myself I don't need it. It’s just about maintaining my speed and keeping that dead weight off, so I don't even risk slowing down. Because once you start letting yourself get soft, it's a slippery slope, you know?
Do you feel like your efforts to avoid gaining weight are affecting your overall quality of life?

Quality of life? I mean... no, not really. I don't see it that way. I know, I know, people are worried. Like I was saying about my wife and my sister, and the guy at the clinic with his whole "safety concern" speech. They all act like the sky is falling, like I'm wasting away or something. But honestly, I figure they're just making way too much of it. They're blowing it out of proportion, because if you actually look at my life, my quality of life, I'm doing great. 

I mean, think about it. I'm still showing up for work every single day, right? I'm not calling in sick, I'm not dragging my feet. I'm under the hoods, pulling transmissions, doing the heavy lifting just like I always have. Maybe even better. And at home, I'm still taking care of what needs doing. I'm mowing the lawn, fixing the gutters, keeping the house running. It's not like I'm lying on the couch all day, too weak to move. And then on the weekends, I'm still out there playing ball. Full-court, running for a couple of hours, keeping up with guys ten years younger than me. 

So when they start talking about my quality of life, or acting like I'm in some kind of danger... I just don't get it. If my life was falling apart, if I couldn't do my job or play my games, then yeah, maybe I'd say it's affecting me. But I'm doing all of that. I'm active, I'm productive, I'm getting things done. So, no, I don't think it's ruining my life or anything. I think it's actually helping me stay on top of things. They just see a number on a scale and panic, but they aren't looking at what I'm actually doing every day.
Do you feel like your fear of gaining weight is affecting your relationship with your wife?

Well, yeah, like I was saying a minute ago, it’s... it’s definitely causing some real tension between us. I mean, I try to explain it to her, but we just go round and round about it. 

Because look, I’m still keeping up with everything at the garage just fine, right? I'm pulling my weight, getting under the hoods, and I'm still out there playing in my basketball league every weekend, running the floor better than I have in years. I'm handling my business. But with my wife... she just can't see past the dinner table. It’s like, because I avoid sitting down for those big, heavy regular family meals she wants us all to have, she thinks something is terribly wrong with me. 

I'll come inside after work, and she'll have this massive spread out—like I said, the casseroles, the pastas, all that heavy stuff—and I just want to grab my plain sliced turkey or a coffee and keep moving. And man, she takes it so personally. She gets this really worried look on her face, and then comes the constant questioning. "Are you okay? You look different. Are you sure you're feeling alright?" It’s just... it's exhausting, honestly. I try to tell her, look at me, I'm working ten-hour days on my feet, I'm playing full-court ball, I'm obviously fine! Do I look like a guy who isn't okay? 

But she just fixates on the fact that I won't sit down and eat a plate of whatever she cooked. She thinks I'm obsessed or something, and I think she's just used to guys my age getting soft and lazy, so she doesn't understand what it takes to actually stay in shape. So, yeah, we argue about it a lot. It definitely puts a wedge in things at home, even though I'm literally doing everything I'm supposed to be doing everywhere else in my life. She just won't let the food thing go.
Are there any activities or hobbies you've stopped doing or avoided because you're worried about gaining weight?

Activities or hobbies? No, man, like I've been trying to explain, I haven't stopped doing the things I actually need or want to do. The garage is full-time, obviously, and I'm still keeping up with that without missing a beat. And my basketball league... I mean, I’m still out there every Saturday morning, and sometimes we even get a pickup game going on Wednesday nights if the guys are around. I'm keeping up with all of that just fine. Better than fine, honestly, because I'm lighter on my feet. 

But... I guess if you count sitting around the dinner table as an activity, then yeah, that's the one thing I avoid. Like I was just saying a minute ago about my wife, it's that whole routine of the regular family meal that I just... I steer clear of it now. I avoid sitting down for those big meals completely. Because if I sit down with them, it's just a whole ordeal, you know? It's not just about the heavy food being passed around, it's the environment. It just causes so much tension at home. 

If I sit there with my plain turkey or just a cup of black coffee while they're eating lasagna or whatever, people just stare. My wife, or my sister if she's visiting, they just keep asking if I'm okay. "Are you sure you're okay? You're not eating, are you feeling alright? You look tired." It's like a broken record. And I'm sitting there thinking, I just worked ten hours and played three games of 21, of course I'm a little tired, but I'm fine! So, yeah, to answer your question, I haven't dropped my real hobbies, the active stuff. But the family dinner thing? I avoid that as much as humanly possible just to get away from the heavy food and to stop the endless questions. I'd rather just keep moving.
Do you think about how your body looks when you're deciding what to eat or how much to eat?

Looks? I mean, it's not like I'm standing in front of the mirror flexing or trying to be some kind of fitness model, you know? I'm a forty-four-year-old mechanic. I don't care about looking pretty. But... if you mean do I think about my body when I'm figuring out what to eat, then yeah, absolutely. But it's more about how I operate, how everything runs. It's like maintenance. 

Because, look, if I step on the scale in the morning and I see it bump up even just a single pound, or... or say I'm getting dressed for the shop and my work jeans feel even a little bit tighter around the waist, it immediately gets in my head. I start thinking I’m getting soft. And once you start getting soft at my age, it’s a slippery slope. 

I start picturing how it's going to affect my whole day. In my line of work, you can't afford to carry extra bulk. I'm sliding under lifts, I'm squeezing between toolboxes and fenders, I'm contorting myself to reach alternators on these new compacts where they give you absolutely zero clearance to work with. If I start getting soft and putting on weight, I know I’ll be slower moving around those cars. I'll be dragging. And it’s the exact same thing on the weekends. If I eat heavy and put on a few pounds, I know I’ll be slower getting up and down the court. Those younger guys in the league, they'll just blow right past me on a fast break, and I'm not going to be the guy gasping for air at half-court. 

So, yeah, when I'm looking at a plate of food, or deciding if I should eat what my wife is pushing on me, I am definitely thinking about my body. I'm thinking, is this going to make my jeans tight? Is this going to slow me down under the hood or on the hardwood? I just refuse to let myself get soft and lose my edge, so I have to be really careful about what I'm putting in the tank. It just makes sense to keep it light.
Do you think you would still be worried about gaining weight if you didn't care about how your body looks?

Yeah, well, exactly, like I was just saying a minute ago, it really isn't about looks for me in the first place. I mean, I'm not trying to win any beauty pageants or get on the cover of a magazine. So, yes, absolutely, I'd still be just as worried. Because, like I told you, it’s all about how I function. It's about the mechanics of it, right? 

If I wake up at 5:30 in the morning, go into the bathroom, and see that scale bump up even a single pound... or, you know, say I'm getting dressed for my shift and my work jeans feel even just a tiny bit tighter around the waist... my brain immediately goes to, "Okay, you're getting soft." And getting soft is the absolute worst thing you can do. It’s not about how the jeans look on me in the mirror, it’s about what that tightness actually means for my day. 

It means extra weight. It means I'm going to be slower. Like I was telling you about the shop—we get these newer cars in, and they pack the engine bays so tight you can barely fit a wrench in there, let alone your whole arm and shoulder. If I’m carrying extra weight, if I've let myself get soft, I'm going to be slower moving around those cars. I'll be bumping into things, struggling to squeeze under the lift, taking twice as long to do a standard job. 

And it's the exact same deal for the basketball court. Even if I didn't care about my looks at all, I'd still care that some twenty-something kid I'm guarding is going to blow right past me for an easy layup because I'm carrying an extra pound or two and can't pivot fast enough. So yeah, the worry doesn't just go away because you take the mirror out of the equation. The worry is about keeping the machine running lean and mean, you know? Because the second you let it slip, the second you feel those jeans get tight, you're already losing a step. And I just... I can't afford to lose a step. Not at the garage, not in the league, not anywhere. It's just too much of a risk to let yourself get heavy.
Are there other areas of your life, besides eating and sports, where you feel like your concerns about weight are affecting your daily activities or decisions?

Other areas? Well... look, like I’ve been saying this whole time, as far as the important stuff goes, I’m totally fine. I’m still keeping up with the garage, pulling my weight, putting in the hours. And the basketball league is going great. I haven't missed a single game. But... I guess if you're asking about other parts of my life, it’s really just the stuff at home. It’s the family dynamic, you know? 

It’s caused a lot of tension at home lately. A lot of tension. And it all comes back to what I was telling you earlier. Because I just absolutely avoid sitting down for those regular family meals now. I just can't do it. My wife, she expects this whole traditional sit-down thing every night, passing around the heavy dishes, the casseroles, the pasta, whatever. And because I won't participate in that—because I’m trying to keep myself running lean—it just turns into this huge ordeal. 

I try to just stay out in the yard, or find something to fix in the basement until they're done eating, but that just makes her mad. And when I do happen to be in the kitchen or if I try to just have a coffee while they eat, it's just constant... people just keep asking if I’m okay. Over and over. "Are you feeling alright? Why aren't you eating with us? Are you sick?" It’s exhausting. I’m perfectly fine, I'm just managing my intake so I don't get soft! But they don't get it. So, yeah, work and sports are a hundred percent, but my home life... it’s definitely strained right now just because I want to skip dinner and avoid the twenty questions.
Are you avoiding any social activities because of your concerns about gaining weight?

Well, I mean, that's kind of exactly what I was just getting at with the whole dinner situation, right? If you mean social activities like... I don't know, hanging out with the guys from the shop or the basketball team, then no, not really. Like I said, I’m still keeping up with the garage perfectly fine, putting in my hours, pulling my weight. And I'm at every single game and practice for my basketball league. I don't miss that stuff. I'll hang out on the court, shoot the breeze with the guys, all of that. I'm still out there doing what I need to do.

But... if you mean social activities that involve sitting around a table? Yeah. Yeah, I avoid those like the plague now. And it’s exactly what I was just telling you about—it has caused so much tension at home. Because a family dinner, or having the in-laws over for a Sunday roast, that's supposed to be a big "social activity" for my wife, right? But for me, it's just a minefield. So I avoid sitting down for those regular family meals entirely. I'll find literally anything else to do. I'll say I need to check the oil in her sedan, or I'll go down to the basement to sort my socket wrenches, just to stay away from the dining room while they're all eating. 

But then, because I'm avoiding the meal, it turns into this whole other social problem where people just keep asking if I’m okay. It's like a broken record. My wife, her sister, the kids—everyone's always coming out to the garage like, "Are you feeling alright? Are you sick? Why aren't you in here eating with us?" It just doesn't stop. I'm completely fine, I'm working hard, I'm playing hard, I just don't want to sit there and be pressured into eating a bunch of heavy casseroles that are going to slow me down. So yeah, I definitely avoid the social stuff at home just so I don't have to deal with everyone interrogating me all night.
Are there any other daily activities, besides eating and playing sports, where you feel like your concerns about gaining weight are affecting your decisions or behavior?

I mean... Doc, I feel like we're going in circles a little bit here, aren't we? Because that's exactly what I've been trying to explain to you for the last ten minutes. If you're asking about my day-to-day decisions outside of what I eat and how I play, it all just comes back to the house. 

Like I said, I’m still keeping up with the garage completely fine. I'm turning wrenches, diagnosing engine codes, doing every single thing I've always done, and the basketball league is solid. I'm not missing a beat there. But my decisions at home? Yeah, they're entirely built around dodging that dinner table. I'm making decisions to, you know, suddenly need to reorganize the entire tool bench in the basement, or deciding I absolutely have to rake the leaves right at 6:00 PM when my wife is pulling some heavy dish out of the oven. 

And like I was just telling you, it has caused so much tension at home. I mean, thick, cut-it-with-a-knife kind of tension. Because I absolutely avoid sitting down for those regular family meals, and then it just snowballs. It turns into this whole big drama where people just keep asking if I’m okay. My wife comes out to the yard, the kids are looking at me weird, and it's just this constant chorus of, "Are you okay? Are you sick? Why are you out here in the dark instead of eating?" It's like, yes, I'm fine, I'm just making a choice for my own performance! I don't need to be weighed down! But they don't see it that way. So my day-to-day behavior at home is basically just... navigating around my own family so I don't have to deal with the food or the constant interrogation. But other than that tension at the house, like I said, everything else is running like a top.
Are there any other parts of your daily routine, outside of meal times and playing basketball, where you feel like your concern about gaining weight is influencing your choices?

Doc, seriously, I... I don't know how many different ways I can say the exact same thing to you. It’s like when a customer brings in a truck complaining about a rattle, and I show them the loose heat shield, I fix it, and they just keep asking me if I'm sure it's not the transmission. No, it's not the transmission! I feel like I've walked you through my whole life here and you're still looking for something that isn't there. 

Let me just spell out my entire routine for you, from top to bottom, okay? Just so we're completely, one hundred percent clear. I wake up at 5:30 AM. I have a black coffee. I'm at the shop by 6:45 to unlock the bays, turn on the air compressors, and get the work orders lined up. From seven until four or five, I am on my feet. I'm under a lift, I'm swapping out brake pads, I'm doing alignments, I'm on the phone arguing with vendors about parts delivery times. None of my choices there have anything to do with my weight. I'm just doing my job and making a living. 

Then, I wash up, I pack my gear, and I head straight to the rec center. I put in my time on the court, I run my drills, I play hard, and I make sure I stay lean so I can keep up with guys who are ten, fifteen years younger than me. 

And *then* I go home. And like I have been telling you for the last twenty minutes, *that* is when the dinner stuff happens. That's when I go out to the yard to rake leaves in the dark, or I go down to the basement to avoid the heavy pasta bakes and the endless questions from my wife and kids. 

That is literally my entire day. Work, basketball, and dodging dinner. There isn't some secret fourth part of my routine. I'm not out there doing anything else. I don't have any other hobbies, and frankly, I don't have the time or the energy for anything else! So no, there are absolutely no other parts of my routine where this is an issue. Just the shop, the court, and the house. That's it. Can we please move on to something else now?
Are there any other aspects of your daily life, outside of food and basketball, where you feel like your fear of gaining weight is affecting your choices or behaviors?

Okay, I... I really don't know what you want me to say here, Doc. I mean, are we speaking the same language? Because I just laid out my entire twenty-four-hour cycle for you, minute by minute, and it feels like you're just reading off a clipboard and asking me the exact same question again. 

No. There is nothing else. Zero. Zip. Nada. I don't know what you think a mechanic's life is like, but I don't exactly have a lot of free time to sit around making... I don't know, lifestyle choices based on my waistline. I'm not going to the mall to try on tailored suits, I'm not going to fancy galas, I'm not joining a yoga studio or whatever it is you're fishing for! 

I wake up, I go to the garage, I bust my knuckles all day fixing suspensions and doing oil changes, I play my basketball so I can stay quick on my feet, and I go home and try to dodge the casserole drama with my wife. That is it. That is the whole picture. I don't have the time, the money, or the energy for anything else. By the time my head hits the pillow, I'm out cold. So unless you're asking if I'm somehow worrying about my weight while I'm completely unconscious and dreaming—which I'm not—then no, there are no other aspects of my life. None at all. 

I really, really need us to move on from this because I feel like I'm just repeating myself until I'm blue in the face, and I'm not sure how else to explain that my life is just work, hoops, and home. That's the whole engine right there. There are no other parts to it.
Are there any other daily activities, besides eating and playing basketball, where you feel like your concern about gaining weight is influencing your choices?

Doc... are you messing with me right now? Is there a hidden camera in this office? Because I swear on my life, you literally just asked me the exact same question word for word. I... I feel like I'm talking to a busted OBD2 scanner that just keeps throwing the exact same error code no matter how many times I clear the system.
